This causes blood pressure to plummet because the cardiovascular system can no longer maintain adequate pressure to perfuse vital organs. To counteract this, you rapidly infuse crystalloid fluids to restore circulating volume and maintain organ perfusion. However, because the vessels are dilated and their walls become more permeable from inflammation, some of this fluid leaks into surrounding tissues—a harmful side effect that can cause dangerous edema, including in the lungs, putting strain on the heart and respiratory system. If fluids alone can’t maintain adequate blood pressure, you then give vasopressors such as norepinephrine to restore vascular tone and squeeze the dilated vessels back toward normal. But timing is critical: Give vasopressors too late, and organs have already suffered irreversible damage from prolonged hypoperfusion; give them too early without adequate fluid resuscitation, and you’re constricting vessels in a volume-depleted patient, potentially worsening tissue perfusion. Meanwhile, antibiotics must be started within the first hour to attack the underlying infection. In other words, a very complex training topic. I explained my thinking about how to treat the patient and purposefully left off a critical part of the explanation about tissue perfusion to see how the AI training agent would respond. With patience and nuanced focus, it said that my thinking was partly right, then asked how I might think about the missing step. This was unscripted AI performing extremely well under highly complex challenges and getting it right! And here is why that matters. We have known since the 1980s that people trained in one-to-one conversational training by a subject matter expert perform two orders of magnitude better than those trained in a classroom. Said another way, the average person trained in one-to-one conversation with an expert will outperform 98 percent of those trained in a classroom. But after forty years of knowing this, we had no practical way to scale expert one-to-one training beyond nuanced adaptive training models. Until now, because of conversational AI. I believe that in the coming year, you will begin to see the early transition to a time when all human teaching is done in partnership with your personal one-to-one AI trainer. One that knows you well, knows the edges of your knowledge, and meets you there. One that remembers all its prior interactions with you as you learned new things. One that never gets tired or frustrated or has a bad day and will work with you any time and any place you choose. One that is both intelligent and also has some form of persistent memory access to all of its interactions with you. It will even give you observational feedback on what times of day you, as an individual, learn best. It is not hard to imagine that time spent in a classroom is about sharing ideas and discoveries from your newly acquired learning. Teachers become guides to your curiosity and AI trainer explorations, driving topics along a logical path for you to walk along with your AI trainer and discover and report back. There’s a certain poetry to it—the intelligence we are helping to emerge in silicon is now circling back to help amplify the minds that created it. The implications for our education systems, our work life, and our nonwork life are not yet fully understood. And so, we begin. We will explore how our brain’s dynamic learning processes gave rise to storytelling, reason, compassion, and error. And how, once we abandoned a database approach to AI and eventually began to mirror elements of our own intelligence processes, we were able to create a new kind of intelligence. This is where our inquiry begins. Not with fear. Not with awe. But with a sense of quiet astonishment at what we have become within the limits of energy in our brains and a deep curiosity about what happens when we leverage what we have learned from the neural model of our brains into a computer with access to massive amounts of energy. To understand how AI mirrors our intelligence, we must first examine what makes human learning so remarkable from the very beginning. Even before we can speak or reason, our brains are already performing computational learning feats that rival the most sophisticated AI systems. In the next chapter, we’ll explore how those learning feats begin—how the earliest human mind, still preverbal, lays the groundwork for all the intelligence that follows. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 3 Born Ready to Learn It begins before memory. Before speech. Before we know the names of things or even understand that things have names. Our DNA does not pass generations of learning down to us but rather passes to us a magical learning architecture capable of learning at an incredible pace, just as it does not pass memories of how the world looks but rather the eye itself . Groundbreaking research by Stanislas Dehaene, PhD, at the Collège de France, has revealed that newborn brains arrive not as blank slates, but as sophisticated prediction engines, prewired and ready to map the world with astonishing efficiency. He is perhaps best known for his work on numeracy, consciousness, and the neurobiological underpinnings of learning—especially in infants and children. His ability to combine rigorous experimental science with sweeping, interdisciplinary insight makes him one of the most influential voices in modern brain science. In his remarkable book How We Learn , Dehaene distills decades of research to reveal that the newborn brain is a learning engine prepared to absorb and adapt with astonishing speed. 19 Sound familiar? We didn’t exactly build AI so much as we gave it the ability to learn. And what comes next is often surprising. Much of what we explore in this chapter comes from Dehaene’s insights, reframing how we understand the handoff from DNA to learning architecture in the human brain—and how that architecture forms the cognitive roots of intelligence.
